Antes los vecinos no se conocían.
Los castellers tenían ___ pisos de personas.

El lunes recibí un correo de una empresa de Múnich. Me ofrecían un trabajo fijo, con un sueldo que en Barcelona solo podría soñar. Aunque llevaba meses buscando algo así, no me alegré tanto como esperaba. Me quedé mirando la pantalla un buen rato.

Esa noche se lo conté a Nuria y a Laia en la terraza. —Si yo fuera tú, lo aceptaría sin pensarlo —dijo Nuria—. Con ese sueldo podrías ahorrar y volver cuando quisieras. Laia, en cambio, no dijo nada durante un rato. Luego me miró y me preguntó: —¿Y tú qué quieres? No lo que deberías querer, sino lo que quieres de verdad.

No supe qué contestar. Como no podía dormir, salí a pasear por Gràcia. Se oían risas en las plazas y alguien tocaba la guitarra. Pensé en mi primer día, cuando no entendía nada y me perdí en el metro. Si alguien me hubiera dicho entonces que algún día me costaría tanto irme, no lo habría creído.

Al día siguiente escribí a la empresa. Les agradecí la oferta y les pregunté si sería posible trabajar en remoto desde Barcelona. Me contestaron que lo {estudiarían|would look into it}. Todavía no sé qué pasará, pero por primera vez tengo claro lo que quiero.

On Monday I got an email from a company in Munich. They were offering me a permanent job, with a salary I could only dream of in Barcelona. Although I'd been looking for something like that for months, I wasn't as happy as I'd expected. I sat staring at the screen for quite a while.

That evening I told Nuria and Laia about it on the terrace. "If I were you, I'd accept it without thinking twice," said Nuria. "With that salary you could save and come back whenever you wanted." Laia, on the other hand, said nothing for a while. Then she looked at me and asked: "And what do you want? Not what you should want, but what you really want."

I didn't know what to answer. As I couldn't sleep, I went for a walk around Gràcia. You could hear laughter in the squares and someone was playing the guitar. I thought about my first day, when I didn't understand anything and got lost in the metro. If someone had told me then that one day I'd find it so hard to leave, I wouldn't have believed it.

The next day I wrote to the company. I thanked them for the offer and asked if it would be possible to work remotely from Barcelona. They replied that they would look into it. I still don't know what will happen, but for the first time I'm clear about what I want.

Fue un martes lluvioso cuando Laia me llamó desde el archivo de la Biblioteca de Catalunya, donde hacía prácticas. —Tienes que venir. No te imaginas lo que he encontrado —me dijo, en voz tan baja que apenas la oí.

Lo que había encontrado era un cuaderno escrito a mano, metido por error en una caja de facturas de 1936. Por muy acostumbrada que estuviera a los documentos antiguos, a Laia le temblaban las manos. Las primeras páginas eran recetas de cocina; ahora bien, a partir de la página veinte, la letra cambiaba y empezaba un diario. Era de una chica de diecisiete años, Mercè, que vivía en Gràcia, a dos calles de nuestro piso.

Pasamos la tarde leyéndolo. Mercè hablaba de los bombardeos con una calma que daba miedo, y eso que, a veces, describía cómo se escondían en el metro. Lo que más me conmovió, sin embargo, no fueron las escenas de guerra, sino lo normal que intentaba ser su vida: los nervios antes de un baile, una pelea con su hermana, un chico que le gustaba.

—Si no lo hubiera abierto por curiosidad, se habría quedado ahí otros noventa años —dijo Laia. De ahí que, a la semana siguiente, la biblioteca decidiera revisar todas las cajas de esa época. Y fue así como, buscando una vida, encontraron cientos.

It was a rainy Tuesday when Laia called me from the archive of the Biblioteca de Catalunya, where she was doing an internship. "You have to come. You can't imagine what I've found," she said, so quietly that I could barely hear her.

What she had found was a handwritten notebook, put by mistake into a box of invoices from 1936. However used she was to old documents, Laia's hands were shaking. The first pages were recipes; from page twenty, however, the handwriting changed and a diary began. It belonged to a seventeen-year-old girl, Mercè, who lived in Gràcia, two streets from our flat.

We spent the afternoon reading it. Mercè wrote about the bombings with a calm that was frightening, even though she sometimes described how they hid in the metro. What moved me most, however, wasn't the war scenes, but how normal she tried to keep her life: the nerves before a dance, a fight with her sister, a boy she liked.

"If I hadn't opened it out of curiosity, it would have stayed there for another ninety years," said Laia. That's why, the following week, the library decided to go through all the boxes from that period. And that's how, looking for one life, they found hundreds.

A year ago, around this time, I landed at El Prat with two suitcases and textbook Spanish. Today I'm writing from the same terrace in Gràcia where Nuria taught me to peel prawns without making a mess – which, incidentally, I still haven't mastered.

In the end, the company in Munich agreed to let me work remotely. I could hardly believe it myself: had I known, I'd have spared myself a few sleepless nights. Whatever happens with the contract next year, I have no more doubts about where I want to be. Laia says I've become "more Mediterranean than the sea"; Pablo, who's still in Madrid, says I've become "a real pain at after-dinner chats". However much they exaggerate, they have a point.

What has changed most, though, isn't where I live, but how I listen. I used to get stressed if I didn't understand a word; now I pay attention to what isn't said: Mrs Rovira's sharp undertone, the "we'll see" that really means "no", the "shall we meet up?" that never comes with a time. In other words: I've learnt the language that lies between the words.

Tonight is the Verbena de Sant Joan. Nuria's grandfather has promised to bring coca and proverbs in equal measure. "Better late than never," he said to me yesterday when I finally gave the neighbour her salt back. He's right. And if someone had told me a year ago that I'd end up quoting proverbs on a roof terrace in Barcelona, I'd have said they were pulling my leg.
